title: A Recent Graduate’s Take On Their First Year In The Insurance Industry
summary: A Recent Graduate’s Take On Their First Year In The Insurance Industry
body_text: Graduating college can be stressful, exciting and filled with uncertainty. For many graduates, it is the first time in their life that school is not the next step. Instead, they must contemplate what career they’d like to pursue. There are many factors to consider when career planning: pay, benefits, stability, location, culture, type of work, etc. Accounting for all these variables can be overwhelming. Where does the insurance industry fit into this complicated process? Why Insurance? Insurance is unique in its stability and job security. It has a reputation for being mostly recession-proof, as it is necessary whether the economy is good or bad. Because insurance is nearly omnipresent, job seekers can find possible employment opportunities anywhere. The industry's strength also promotes competitive salaries and benefits, especially in sales, underwriting, management and actuarial work. The insurance landscape can be overwhelming due to its complex terminology, acronyms, and numerous industry concepts. Additionally, insurance involves many players and layers, requiring a solid understanding of the structure and roles within the industry. These roles require various skills, attracting people with well-rounded competencies like math, communication, critical thinking and logic. Insurance is also modernizing in many exciting ways, particularly in technology like artificial intelligence and data analytics. For some younger professionals, this is a great opportunity to be at the forefront of modern business.

title: Sales Tax for AI Agents and Agentic Workflows: What Developers Need to Know (2026)
summary: Read Sales Tax for AI Agents and Agentic Workflows: What Developers Need to Know (2026) on the Afternoon blog
body_text: As AI development shifts toward agentic workflows, many startups now build software that orchestrates or extends the capabilities of large language models from providers like OpenAI and Anthropic. These businesses, whether offering autonomous agents, workflow automation tools, or AI copilots, often fall within existing digital service tax frameworks. Understanding where and how sales tax applies is essential for maintaining compliance as your user base grows across states. This guide covers: When OpenAI and Anthropic charge sales tax on API usage When your own AI agent or automation service becomes taxable How to determine your registration and filing responsibilities Best practices for compliance as an AI-focused business If you’d prefer to automate your registrations, filings, and bookkeeping, Afternoon.co helps SaaS and AI companies stay compliant in all 50 states. The three layers of sales tax exposure for AI-driven businesses From a compliance standpoint, an AI company typically operates across three layers of potential sales tax responsibility: Purchasing: paying for API access and infrastructure (e.g., OpenAI or Anthropic) Selling: charging customers for access to your own software or workflows Filing: reporting and remitting tax to states where you have nexus Each layer is governed by separate rules and obligations. 1. Tax on API usage Both OpenAI and Anthropic treat API usage as a taxable digital service in certain jurisdictions. OpenAI API Pricing excludes sales tax by default Tax is applied based on your billing address A valid U.S. sales tax exemption certificate can remove the charge if applicable Reference: OpenAI Sales Tax FAQ Anthropic API Tax is applied based on your account’s business address and tax ID Entering your business tax ID ensures correct VAT or sales tax treatment Reference: Anthropic – How Taxes Are Calculated In short: taxes collected by API providers apply only to your vendor relationship with them, not to your end-customer transactions. Talk to a sales tax expert Get guidance tailored to your business 2. Tax on your AI agent or workflow sales When customers pay to use your AI-driven software, whether for automation, data generation, or conversational interfaces, those transactions are typically considered taxable digital services under many state tax codes. How states classify AI services While most states haven’t created an “AI service” category, they apply existing frameworks for digital and cloud software: Category Description Taxability (Common States) SaaS (Software as a Service) Customers access software remotely (most AI agents fit here) Taxable in 30+ states including NY, TX, WA, MA ( see full guide ) Digital Automated Services Software performs automated tasks or generates data Taxable in WA Data Processing or Information Services AI models transform or analyze data Taxable in TX and NY Custom Services / Consulting Human work with minimal automation Often exempt If your platform takes user input, processes it through OpenAI or Anthropic’s models, and delivers an output through your own interface or workflow, most states treat that as SaaS or a digital automated service, both generally taxable categories. Example scenario You pay OpenAI $1,000/month for API usage (taxed by OpenAI) You charge users $20/month for access to your AI workflow platform States like WA or TX require you to collect and remit sales tax on those user transactions In non-taxable states (like CA or FL), you may not charge tax but must still track sales for nexus thresholds 3. Registration, collection, and filing Even though your API providers may collect sales tax from you, your business has its own obligations for sales to customers. Step 1: Register where you have nexus Economic nexus laws require registration once you exceed certain thresholds (commonly $100,000 in revenue or 200 transactions per year) within a state. Your AI service revenue counts toward these thresholds regardless of upstream taxes. Step 2: Collect the correct tax Use a tax engine such as Stripe Tax, Avalara, or your accounting platform to determine rates by customer address. Always display a separate “Sales Tax” line item on invoices or receipts. Step 3: File and remit File returns, monthly or quarterly depending on volume, in each state where you’re registered. Maintain records of: Total sales by state Taxable vs. exempt revenue Tax collected and remitted Copies of exemption certificates (if applicable) Common misconceptions “OpenAI already collected tax from me.” Incorrect: those charges apply to your API purchases, not to your customer-facing revenue. “AI tools aren’t taxable because they’re new.” False: most states apply existing SaaS or digital service rules to AI-driven offerings. “I don’t need to worry until I’m large.” Partially true: but many startups cross nexus thresholds quickly through online sales and subscriptions. Quick reference: Where AI agents and workflows are likely taxable State Classification Taxable? Notes Washington Digital Automated Service Yes Retail sales tax applies Texas Data Processing Yes 80% taxable under state rules New York Information Service / SaaS Yes Sales tax on remote software California SaaS (remote access) No Track for nexus only Massachusetts SaaS Yes 6.25% sales tax Illinois (Chicago) Cloud Service Yes Local cloud tax applies Florida SaaS No Exempt digital service Pennsylvania SaaS Yes Taxable digital product For a comprehensive state-by-state overview, see Afternoon’s SaaS Sales Tax Guide . Best practices for AI companies Track where your customers are located to determine tax sourcing Keep API costs and customer revenue separate in bookkeeping Monitor thresholds and register as soon as you establish nexus Collect valid resale or exemption certificates from B2B clients Use automated tools or providers like Afternoon.co to manage compliance Review the 2026 SaaS Sales Tax Guide for evolving state rules FAQs Does OpenAI charge sales tax for API usage? Yes, based on your billing address. You can request exemption if eligible. Does Anthropic charge tax for API credits? Yes. Tax is determined by your account location and business tax ID. If OpenAI or Anthropic charge me tax, do I still need to collect from users? Yes. Their taxes apply to your purchases, not your customer transactions. Are AI agents considered SaaS? Generally yes, if users access your software remotely, states categorize it as SaaS or a digital service. What happens if I don’t register? Unregistered sellers risk penalties, back taxes, and potential compliance issues during fundraising or acquisition. References OpenAI – U.S. Sales Tax Exemption Anthropic – Tax Calculation FAQ Afternoon – SaaS Sales Tax Guide

title: Klarna gets physical with lululemon, launching in-store in the UK & Germany | Klarna International
body_text: London, July 22, 2026 — Klarna, the global digital bank and flexible payments provider, is expanding in-store with lululemon in the UK and Germany, giving customers the same flexibility on the shop floor that they already enjoy online and marking a significant step in Klarna’s push into physical retail. Paying in-store with Klarna at lululemon is simple. At checkout, shoppers simply scan a QR code with their phone and pay using the Klarna app. There's no need to apply for anything in the queue or carry a separate card. In a few seconds, customers can spread the cost into interest-free payments or delay payment for a month — so they can buy what they came for, on their terms. Klarna and lululemon have offered shoppers flexible payments online for more than five years. Bringing Klarna to the till is a natural next step in that relationship and reflects Klarna's strategic move beyond the browser, with in-person spending estimated at about $28 trillion a year globally, nearly four times the amount spent online. “Shopping shouldn't be less flexible the moment you walk into a store," said Klarna Chief Commercial Officer David Sykes. "We've spent years making online checkout smarter, and now we're bringing that same freedom to the till. Whether you're picking up your kit in person or ordering it online, you should be able to pay the way that best works for you.” Klarna is available now in-store at lululemon in the UK and Germany, enabled through lululemon's integration with payments platform Adyen.

title: Vera Health Accelerates Its Expansion in Spain: One in Seven Doctors Already Use Vera
summary: elEconomista and El Español each published a feature today on Vera Health's expansion in Spain, a market where one in seven doctors already uses the platform. Almost all of them arrived the same way: another doctor recommended it.
body_text: Madrid, July 16, 2026. Vera Health, the clinical search engine that gives healthcare professionals evidence-based answers to any medical question in seconds, is accelerating its expansion across Spain and Italy after becoming one of the fastest-growing clinical AI tools in Europe. Today, elEconomista and El Español each published a feature on how the company reached this point and what it wants to build alongside Spanish clinicians. One in seven doctors in Spain already use Vera Roughly one in seven practicing doctors in Spain now uses Vera to search, appraise, and apply medical evidence at the point of care. In Italy, it is one in nine. That growth happened without a single marketing campaign, driven almost entirely by word of mouth between clinicians and everyday use. None of those doctors arrived through a contract signed in an office. They arrived because a colleague showed them an answer. That detail explains much of what elEconomista and El Español describe today. "Spain has become one of Vera's fastest-growing markets anywhere in the world. The fact that one in seven doctors already uses the platform shows that clinicians are actively looking for trustworthy AI tools: tools that are transparent, evidence-based, and designed to support rather than replace clinical judgment," said Taieb Bennani, co-founder of Vera Health. The platform is now used by more than 400,000 doctors worldwide, who ask more than three million clinical questions every month. Evidence first, then the answer Founded in 2024 by Taieb Bennani and Maxime Allouch, Vera has built what it describes as "the Google of medicine": a clinical search engine that retrieves, ranks, and synthesizes the highest-quality medical evidence in seconds. The difference from a general-purpose AI assistant is not one of degree but of method. Instead of generating answers from memory, Vera analyzes more than 60 million peer-reviewed publications, clinical guidelines, drug references, and medical monographs, links every statement to verifiable sources, and grades the strength of the evidence behind each recommendation. Each source is rated against multiple criteria: study design, the Oxford CEBM level, the ACEP classification, journal quality, and citation impact. The clinician sees not only what the evidence says, but how solid it is. "Our ambition is simple: when a doctor has a question, the best available evidence should be within reach in a matter of seconds," says Taieb Bennani. Who decides what makes a good clinical answer Vera was first developed alongside emergency physicians, where every second counts. That is the origin of its strategic alliance with the American College of Emergency Physicians (ACEP), one of the largest medical societies in the United States with more than 40,000 members, whose clinical policies are integrated directly into the platform. The company's Clinical Council includes physicians from Harvard, Columbia, Yale, Mayo Clinic, and the University of Virginia, who continuously review the app and collectively define what constitutes a high-quality clinical answer. "If we can help emergency physicians find the right evidence in seconds, we can help every clinician. Spain and Italy mark an important new chapter in building a truly European ecosystem for trustworthy clinical AI," adds Maxime Allouch, co-founder of Vera Health. Over the coming months, Vera Health will expand its collaboration with hospitals, healthcare providers, medical societies, and scientific institutions across Spain and Italy. The credit belongs to clinicians This recognition belongs to the doctors who open Vera every day and who, at some point, showed it to a colleague. Vera grows because of them. And if it helps more healthcare professionals and more patients today, it is thanks to them. Thank you. Coverage in the Spanish press Two outlets are reporting the news today. title: Flexport Appoints Rick Tang as General Manager of Greater China
summary: Discover Flexport APIs and EDIs to speed, scale, and optimize your supply chain. Developer tools make it easy to instantly access logistics data and vital cargo and global trade documentation in the Flexport Platform or your ERP.
body_text: Shanghai, China, July 7, 2026 — Flexport, a global leader in supply chain technology, is announcing the appointment of Rick Tang as General Manager of Greater China. Tang brings more than 27 years of experience in global freight forwarding and logistics leadership at DHL companies and will focus on driving growth and strengthening Flexport's presence across China. "Greater China is one of the most important markets for global trade, and customers there are looking for faster, more flexible ways to manage complex supply chains," said Daniel Sanvicente, Senior Vice President of Asia-Pacific at Flexport. "Rick brings the regional expertise and customer relationships to help more businesses in Greater China benefit from Flexport’s technology and global network, while accelerating our growth across the region." Tang most recently served as Area Director, Greater China at Hillebrand Gori, a DHL company, and before that, Head of Ocean Freight, China & Hong Kong at DHL Global Forwarding. During his 27-year career with DHL Global Forwarding and its predecessor companies, Danzas and AEI, he held leadership roles across air freight, ocean freight, operations, strategy, and commercial management in Shanghai, Chengdu, Ningbo, Xiamen, and Chicago. "I've spent my career helping Chinese companies expand globally, and today they are navigating more complex supply chains and rising expectations for speed and visibility," said Tang. "Whether they're entering new markets, managing multiple trade lanes, or looking for greater visibility and control, companies need a logistics partner built for the way global trade works today. Flexport combines AI-powered logistics, customs expertise, and global execution on a single platform to help businesses operate more efficiently." Tang’s appointment comes as Chinese exporters diversify into new markets and rethink how they manage global logistics. Flexport’s platform connects freight, inventory, and customs into one system, helping businesses make faster decisions and keep goods moving across international markets. In 2025, Flexport shipped across 135 countries and today operates more than 45 offices around the world. About Flexport We believe trade can move the human race forward. That's why since our founding in 2013, it's our mission to make global commerce so easy there is more of it. Flexport is the tech-driven platform for global logistics—empowering buyers, sellers and their logistics partners with the technology and services to grow and innovate. Flexport was one of CNBC's Disruptor 50 Companies as well as one of Fast Company's Most Innovative Companies. Trusted by more than 10,000 brands, Flexport connects every step of the supply chain from factory floor to customer door—making it easy for businesses to ship anywhere, sell everywhere, and grow faster.

title: Catching up with returning ProQRian René Beukema
summary: In this personal interview, we speak to ProQR’s Chief Corporate Development Officer & General Counsel, René Beukema on his return to ProQR.
body_text: Listen Interview with ProQR's Chief Corporate Development Officer Catching up with returning ProQRian René Beukema Share Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Email 09 February 2023 In this personal interview, we speak to ProQR’s Chief Corporate Development Officer & General Counsel, René Beukema on his return to ProQR. What attracted you to come back to ProQR? What impact are you hoping to make? “I am extremely passionate about ProQR’s focus on developing RNA technologies that allow us to develop potentially life-changing medicines for patients with high unmet medical needs and believe I can make meaningful contributions helping the company execute against its strategy of accelerating our next-generation RNA-base editing platform technology, Axiomer™. I am in the unique position of bringing experiences from my previous role at ProQR, including an extensive understanding of the Company’s purpose and culture, as well as those gained through other M&A, capital markets, and corporate development roles to help us advance to the next stage of our evolution.” In your opinion, how has ProQR changed since you were last part of the company? “ProQR’s experiences over the last few years have enabled us to hone our strengths and refine our strategy to have an impact for as many patients as possible. By focusing our efforts and establishing strategic partnerships like we did with Lilly , ProQR is in new phase that prioritizes our Axiomer RNA-base editing technology.” I look forward to the day when the potential of Axiomer is realized and we are bringing transformative medicines to patients in need. What are the short and long-term goals you are looking to accomplish with your team? “In the near term, I want to help our team bring in the next phase of ProQR’s journey by accelerating the growth our Axiomer platform. This includes communicating our vision and plans for Axiomer to both internal and external stakeholders. Importantly, we are also focused on seeking a strategic partner for our ophthalmology assets, who can take these programs forward. Over the long term, I want to see our RNA platform playing a key role in the development of therapeutics for patients suffering from diseases with high unmet need.” How do you distinguish ProQR from other RNA therapy companies? “ProQR is pioneering a next-generation RNA technology called Axiomer, which could potentially yield a new class of medicines. Our proprietary Axiomer RNA-editing technology enables your body to treat disease, by using editing oligonucleotides to attract ADAR (Adenosine Deaminase Acting on RNA) at a specific location in an RNA to make an edit. At ProQR, our deep commitment to these types of advancements is what sets us apart. The offices at our headquarters in Leiden (Netherlands) are centered around the laboratories where our scientists develop our novel RNA therapies, putting science, literally, at the heart of what we do.” For you personally, what are your greatest hopes for the business? “I look forward to the day when the potential of Axiomer is realized and we are bringing transformative medicines to patients in need. I am confident ProQR will be an industry leader in the years to come at the forefront of RNA-based medicines.” About the Axiomer technology At ProQR we invented the Axiomer™ technology that enables single base editing to target currently untreatable diseases. title: ANGEL FOUNDERS TRANSFER MORE THAN 10 MILLION SUPER-VOTING SHARES TO ANGEL MISSION TRUST TO PRESERVE COMPANY’S MISSION FOR GENERATIONS | Angel
summary: Angel (NYSE: ANGX) – a media and technology company successfully pioneering a first of its kind audience-driven studio model in which Angel Guild members wat...
body_text: ANGEL FOUNDERS TRANSFER MORE THAN 10 MILLION SUPER-VOTING SHARES TO ANGEL MISSION TRUST TO PRESERVE COMPANY’S MISSION FOR GENERATIONS Provo, UT—July 2, 2026 Angel (NYSE: ANGX) – a media and technology company successfully pioneering a first of its kind audience-driven studio model in which Angel Guild members watch, screen and vote on which films and television series get distributed in theaters and on the Angel platform – today announced that Angel Co-Founders Neal Harmon and Jeffrey Harmon have irrevocably transferred more than 10 million shares of super-voting class B Angel stock to the Angel Mission Trust. This creates a perpetual stewardship structure that preserves the company’s independence, values, and mission to amplify light for generations to come. As Angel Guild members vote, they pledge to choose excellent entertainment that is true, honest, noble, just, authentic, lovely, admirable, or joyful. This is what it means to amplify light. “Our heroes are the Disney brothers,” said Neal Harmon, Angel Co-Founder and CEO, “And while Disney still has an amazing heritage, we’ve all watched the company’s mission drift after Walt and Roy were gone. Our hope is that this Trust will help Angel’s mission last long after we are gone.” The Trust draws inspiration from mission-driven companies such as Patagonia, Hershey, and Rolex. It is irrevocable, with a professional Trustee, independent Enforcer, and Trust Stewardship Committee. All decisions prioritize generational mission integrity and long-term performance over short-term gains. Angel will continue to innovate through its pioneering Angel Guild model while the Angel Mission Trust provides enduring governance. About Angel Studios, Inc. Angel (NYSE: ANGX) is a media and technology company successfully pioneering a first-of-its-kind audience-driven studio model. Founded by brothers who struggled to find films they could watch with their children, Angel was built on the belief that there was a global audience hungry for values-driven storytelling that amplifies light, celebrates hope, and inspires the moral imagination of viewers. That audience became the Angel Guild, a rapidly growing community of 2.6 million paying members who watch, screen, and vote on which films and television series get produced and distributed in theaters and on the Angel app. Angel has achieved the highest audience satisfaction scores in the industry* and the highest average domestic box office per title among all independent studios since 2023. It has done so while evolving a new economic model that shares profits more fully with filmmakers. For more information, visit www.angel.com. Contacts: David Shane Corporate Communications press@angel.com Luk Janssens Investor Relations InvestorRelations@angel.com * www.rottentomatoes.com Popcornmeter (Data sourced April 22, 2026)

title: 7 customizable internal tools for B2B agencies
summary: Compare Airtable, Retool, Softr, Appsmith, monday.com, and Noloco to find the right internal tool for your growing agency's delivery workflows.
body_text: Your account manager built a client tracker in Airtable last spring. Your ops lead built a separate resourcing sheet in a different Airtable base three months later. Somewhere in between, someone spun up a Retool dashboard for finance that nobody outside finance can open. None of these tools talk to each other, and every new hire needs a fifteen minute tour just to find where anything lives. This is what "internal tools" usually looks like at a growing agency: useful pieces, built fast, going in different directions. The fix isn't fewer tools. It's picking one flexible enough to hold client data, project data, and financial data in the same place, without needing an engineer on staff to maintain it. This guide compares seven tools agencies use to build customizable internal tools, ranked on how well they fit agency delivery work specifically (not general internal tooling for a product company), and what each one is genuinely best at. TL;DR The average company now runs 101 apps, and that number just cracked 100 for the first time, according to Okta's 2025 Businesses at Work report . Agencies feel this acutely because every new client can mean another spreadsheet or tool. Airtable, Softr, and Glide are the fastest way to get a working internal tool live, but they were built as app layers, not as a single system of record for a whole agency. Retool and Appsmith are built for engineering teams building internal dashboards, not for non-technical agency owners managing client delivery. monday.com is a strong internal work tracker but treats client access as an add-on, not a first-class feature. Noloco is built specifically to be the operating layer for client-facing service businesses: internal tools, client portals, and permissions in one connected system. What makes an internal tool "customizable" for a B2B agency? A customizable internal tool is software your team builds around your actual delivery process, instead of adapting your process to fit someone else's template. For an agency, that usually means a system that can hold clients, projects, tasks, time, and invoices together, and can be reshaped as your service offering changes. Generic project management software gives you a fixed structure: boards, tickets, or docs. A customizable internal tool gives you a blank data model you configure yourself, which matters because agency delivery rarely looks the same across two clients, let alone two verticals. How do you choose between building and buying an internal tool? Most agencies don't choose once. They start by hacking together a spreadsheet, move to a no-code app layer like Airtable or Softr once volume grows, and eventually hit a ceiling where they need permissions, automations, and a client-facing layer all working together. The decision point is usually volume and stakes: once you're running more than a handful of active clients, or once a client asks to see live status themselves, ad hoc tools stop being safe. That's the moment to compare dedicated platforms rather than stacking another spreadsheet on top of the last one. Which internal tools should growing agencies compare in 2026? Here's a quick-reference view before the detailed breakdown below. Rank Tool Best for 1 Airtable Flexible data layer for teams already comfortable with spreadsheets 2 Softr Fast, simple front ends on top of an existing Airtable base 3 Glide Lightweight mobile-first internal apps 4 Retool Engineering teams building internal dashboards on existing databases 5 Appsmith Open-source, self-hosted internal tools for technical teams 6 monday.com Internal task and workflow tracking for teams that don't need client access 7 Noloco One system for internal tools, client portals, and delivery workflows together ‍ 1. Airtable Airtable is the closest thing to a common language among growing agencies. It's a flexible spreadsheet-database hybrid that most operations leads already know how to use, and a huge share of agency stacks start here for tracking clients, projects, or content calendars. Where it falls short for agency delivery: Airtable's native interfaces weren't built for granular, client-facing permissions, and once an agency needs a real portal (branded, with fields hidden per client), most teams pair it with a front-end layer. Many agencies keep Airtable as the data layer and add an interface on top rather than replacing it. 2. Softr Softr is built to turn an Airtable base into a usable web app fast, which makes it a natural next step once a spreadsheet-based process needs a real interface. It's approachable for non-technical builders and quick to launch. The tradeoff is depth. Softr's permission model and workflow automation are lighter than what agencies need once client portals involve billing, approvals, or multi-step processes, so more complex delivery workflows often outgrow it. 3. Glide Glide specializes in mobile-first internal apps, which suits agencies with field teams or staff who need to log data from a phone rather than a desktop. Setup is quick and the mobile experience is genuinely strong. It's a narrower tool than the others on this list. Glide is a good fit for a single mobile-first use case, but agencies looking for one system to run clients, projects, and finances together will hit its ceiling quickly. 4. Retool Retool is built for engineering teams that need to build internal dashboards and admin panels on top of an existing database quickly. It's powerful in the hands of a developer and widely used inside larger software companies. For most agencies, that's exactly the problem: Retool assumes someone on the team can write queries and manage a technical build. Agencies in the professional services space, per the common ICP profile , typically don't have in-house engineering, which makes Retool a harder fit than a true no-code option. 5. Appsmith Appsmith is an open-source alternative to Retool, popular with technical teams that want to self-host their internal tools rather than pay for a hosted platform. It offers similar dashboard-building capability with more control over deployment. Like Retool, it's designed for developers. Self-hosting also adds ongoing maintenance work, which runs counter to what most agencies actually want: less infrastructure to manage, not more. 6. monday.com monday.com is a mainstream work management tool many agencies already use for internal task tracking, and its visual boards are easy for non-technical teams to adopt. Brand familiarity is a real advantage; most new hires already know how to use it. It was designed for internal team productivity first. Client-facing access is possible but sits on top as an add-on rather than a foundation, and per-seat pricing can get expensive fast as an agency adds external users alongside its internal team. 7. Noloco Noloco is built specifically for growing service businesses that need internal tools and client-facing access to run on the same system, rather than stitching a data layer, a front end, and a client portal together from three different vendors. Agencies already on Airtable can connect it directly and add real interfaces, granular permissions, and automations on top, without migrating data. Redrock Entertainment used Noloco on top of Airtable to run an operating system for more than 100 users, and cut software costs by 60% in the process, according to Jesse VanDenGooy, Technology Solutions Architect at Redrock Entertainment. That's the pattern Noloco is built around: one connected system for the team internally, with client collaboration built in rather than bolted on through a separate portal tool. How do these tools compare on cost, client access, and setup time? Tool Needs coding skills Client-facing portals Granular permissions Built-in automations Airtable ❌ No ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Basic Softr ❌ No ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Basic Glide ❌ No ❌ No ⚠️ Limited ⚠️ Basic Retool ✅ Yes ❌ No ✅ Yes ⚠️ Basic Appsmith ✅ Yes ❌ No ✅ Yes ⚠️ Basic monday.com ❌ No ⚠️ Add-on ⚠️ Role-based only ✅ Yes Noloco ❌ No ✅ Yes, included ✅ Field and record level ✅ Yes ‍ How do you decide which tool fits your agency? If your team is a handful of people testing a specific workflow, Airtable, Softr, or Glide will get you there fast without much setup cost. Start there if you're not yet feeling operational pain. If you have engineers on staff and the internal tool never needs to touch a client, Retool or Appsmith give that team full control. That's a rare setup for a professional services firm without in-house IT, though, which is most of this audience. If your agency is past 10 to 15 people, juggling multiple client-facing tools, or fielding requests from clients who want their own visibility into project status, that's the point to look at a platform like Noloco's Agency OS , which combines the interface builder , permissions , and workflow automation agencies need under one system instead of three. Final thoughts Most agencies don't choose an internal tool once. They outgrow one and move to the next, usually at the exact moment a client asks for visibility the current setup can't safely provide. Knowing where each tool's ceiling sits before you build on it saves a migration later. The tools on this list solve real, different problems. Airtable, Softr, and Glide are fast starting points. Retool and Appsmith suit engineering-led teams. monday.com is a solid internal tracker. For agencies that need internal tools and client portals running on the same connected system, that's the specific gap Noloco is built to close. Frequently asked questions What counts as an internal tool for an agency? An internal tool is any custom application a team builds to manage its own operations, such as a client tracker, resourcing dashboard, or approval workflow, rather than software bought off the shelf for a single purpose. Do agencies need developers to build internal tools? Not with no-code platforms. Tools like Airtable, Softr, Glide, and Noloco are designed for non-technical builders, while Retool and Appsmith generally assume someone on the team can write code or queries. Can internal tools also work as client portals? Some can. Airtable and Softr offer limited external sharing, while platforms built around granular permissions, like Noloco, let agencies expose specific fields and records to clients without giving them access to internal data. How long does it take to build a working internal tool? This varies by platform and complexity, but no-code tools generally get a basic version live in days rather than the weeks or months custom development requires. Is it cheaper to build an internal tool or buy a pre-built one? Building gives more control over fit but adds ongoing maintenance time. Pre-built platforms cost more upfront but reduce the time a team spends maintaining and rebuilding tools as the agency's process changes. What happens when an agency outgrows Airtable as its main system? Most agencies either add an interface layer on top of Airtable to keep using it as the data source, or consolidate into a broader operating system once managing multiple disconnected tools becomes the bigger cost. Client portals : what a branded, permission-controlled client portal actually needs to include. Permissions : how field and record level access works for external users. Workflow automation : building automations that match how your agency actually delivers work. Agency OS : the full picture of running team and client work in one connected system. See it on your own data. Book a walkthrough of how Noloco's Agency OS handles internal tools, client portals, and permissions out of the box, the same setup that helped Redrock Entertainment cut software costs by 60% while supporting more than 100 users. ‍

title: Chart of Accounts for SaaS Startups: A 2026 Template
summary: Build a chart of accounts for SaaS that holds up at audit. See revenue segmented for ASC 606, hosting in COGS, and S&M split from G&A.
body_text: What Is a SaaS Chart of Accounts? A SaaS chart of accounts is the master index of every general ledger account, organized into the GAAP financial-statement elements and arranged by a numbering convention so the financials roll up automatically. The conceptual basis for those elements is FASB Concepts Statement No. 6, Elements of Financial Statements , which defines assets, liabilities, equity, revenues, expenses, gains, and losses. Every account in a SaaS COA is, at root, one of those elements. The numbering is just how you keep them in order. What makes a SaaS chart distinct is not the elements but the account-level detail inside them. A software company carries deferred revenue, accrued revenue, and deferred cost of revenue, and almost never carries inventory. Its revenue lines split recurring subscription income from one-time services and usage. Its cost of revenue is dominated by cloud hosting, not raw materials. A generic QuickBooks default template fails the test. It has no deferred revenue account, no hosting COGS line, and a single undifferentiated “Sales” account. As Kruze Consulting frames it, an analyst should be able to read your industry off your chart. Account counts scale with stage. A seed-stage company runs lean at roughly 30 to 40 accounts. By Series A ($1M to $5M ARR) that expands to 50 to 70 with revenue breakouts and COGS detail, and Series B and beyond often reaches 80 to 100 or more once departmental tracking and multi-entity subaccounts come into play, per DualEntry . The structure stays constant. The granularity grows. The SaaS COA Structure The standard SaaS chart of accounts uses a four-digit numbering convention where the first digit identifies the financial-statement class, with accounts running in balance-sheet-first, income-statement-second order. NetSuite, QuickBooks Online, and most mid-market ledgers share this logic. In NetSuite’s own convention , all accounts beginning with 1 are assets, all beginning with 2 are liabilities, and so on, which keeps reporting consistent across periods. QuickBooks Online uses the same four-digit default once account numbers are enabled under Account and Settings, per Intuit . Here is the high-level SaaS chart of accounts template, with the caveat that exact range assignment varies by firm and tool while the classification logic does not. Range Class SaaS-specific accounts 1000-1999 Assets Cash, AR, accrued / unbilled revenue (contract asset), deferred cost of revenue, deferred commissions, capitalized software, fixed assets 2000-2999 Liabilities AP, accrued liabilities, deferred revenue current, deferred revenue long-term, debt 3000-3999 Equity Common stock, preferred, APIC, retained earnings 4000-4999 Revenue Subscription, expansion, usage, setup, professional services, contra-revenue 5000-5999 COGS / Cost of revenue Hosting, embedded third-party software, CS / implementation labor, payment processing, amortization of capitalized software 6000-6999 Operating expense: R&D Engineering wages, dev tools, contractor engineering 7000-7999 Operating expense: S&M Sales wages, commissions, ad spend, marketing tools, events 8000-8999 Operating expense: G&A Exec, finance, HR, legal, rent, insurance, software 9000-9999 Other income / expense, tax Interest, FX, gains and losses, income tax Where a firm draws the lines varies. Some collapse all operating expense into one band, and Kruze uses six-digit numbers with S&M and R&D in adjacent 600000 and 700000 ranges. The number itself is cosmetic. What matters is that each account is correctly classified, because that classification drives gross margin, operating margin, and every benchmark above and below them. Two design rules apply across both tools. First, leave gaps between account numbers so related accounts can be inserted later without renumbering history. If your COGS accounts run 5000 to 5050, start the next at 5100, not 5051. Second, use parent and child subaccounts for discipline rather than a flat sprawl. QuickBooks Online writes this as Hosting:AWS , and NetSuite points a child at its parent via the subaccount field, per the NetSuite chart-of-accounts management guide . SaaS-Specific Application The SaaS accounting structure earns its keep in three account blocks: revenue segmented for ASC 606, COGS that isolates delivery cost, and operating expense split to match SaaS benchmarks. This is where a generic template and a purpose-built one diverge. Revenue accounts (4000s): segment by ARR type, tied to ASC 606 SaaS revenue must be segmented by recognition pattern, because ASC 606 cadence differs by stream and investors compute retention off the breakout. A workable block: 4000 Subscription revenue (recurring, recognized ratably over the contract term) 4100 Expansion / upsell revenue (recurring, separated so you can compute net revenue retention) 4200 Usage / overage revenue (recognized as the usage is incurred) 4300 Implementation / setup revenue (recognized over the period benefited, or at a point in time if a distinct performance obligation) 4400 Professional services revenue (recognized as services are delivered) 4900 Contra-revenue: discounts and refunds Each stream maps to a different ASC 606 treatment, which is why blending them into one “Revenue” account is both an audit and an analytics failure. The AICPA Audit and Accounting Guide: Revenue Recognition devotes Chapter 9 to software entities, walking through when a setup fee is a distinct obligation versus a material right. The reason expansion revenue gets its own account is metrics, not aesthetics. Net revenue retention is (beginning ARR minus churned minus contraction plus expansion) divided by beginning ARR, excluding new-customer revenue, per ChartMogul . Gross revenue retention strips out expansion and caps at 100%. If new, expansion, and base subscription all land in one account, neither number can be computed from the ledger. That metric only exists if the COA was built to produce it. COGS accounts (5000s): isolate the cost of delivering the product SaaS cost of revenue is the single largest lever on gross margin, so the COGS block must capture every cost tied to delivering the product and nothing else. The rule is mechanical. If a cost is incurred to deliver the running product to existing customers, it is COGS. If it is incurred to build, sell, or run the company, it is operating expense, per The SaaS CFO . A SaaS COGS block: 5000 Hosting and cloud infrastructure (AWS, GCP, Azure production environments) 5100 Third-party software embedded in the product (data, monitoring, security APIs that ship inside the product) 5200 Customer success and implementation labor (the delivery headcount, not post-sale account management that is really sales) 5300 Payment processing fees (Stripe and similar, where you are the merchant of record) 5400 Professional services COGS (labor to deliver paid services revenue) 5500 Amortization of capitalized software (the periodic charge on internally developed software) The consequence of getting this wrong is direct. SaaS gross margins benchmark at 71 to 72% on a blended basis, with the strongest companies above 80%, per the High Alpha / OpenView SaaS Benchmarks . Drop hosting into operating expense and your gross margin reads artificially high, which dies in diligence. Drop a sales commission into COGS and your margin reads artificially low. Both distortions survive only until someone who knows SaaS reads the statements. Operating expense accounts (6000s to 8000s): split S&M, R&D, G&A Operating expense must split into R&D, S&M, and G&A, with Customer Success sitting in COGS or G&A depending on whether the function delivers the product or manages the account. The split is not optional for a company that reports against benchmarks. The R&D bucket (6000s) carries engineering wages, dev tooling, and contractor engineering, and it matters beyond reporting. Domestic engineering wages are the core of the qualified research expense base, and software development is treated as Section 174 research expenditure. New Section 174A permanently restored immediate expensing of domestic R&E for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024, while foreign R&E still amortizes over 15 years, per Grant Thornton . A chart that cleanly isolates domestic engineering wages makes both the credit calculation and the 174A treatment far easier to support, which is exactly why Indinero’s business tax services treat the COA design and the return as one workflow. S&M (7000s) holds sales wages, commissions, advertising, and events. Capitalized commissions under ASC 340-40 sit on the balance sheet as a deferred cost asset, not here, with only the amortization flowing through. G&A (8000s) covers executive, finance, HR, and legal wages, rent, insurance, and general software. S&M must be separated from G&A because the magic number, CAC payback, and the Rule of 40 are all computed off isolated sales and marketing spend. Lump S&M into a generic SG&A account and none of those numbers can be pulled from the ledger. The same data feeds your board reporting, which is why fractional CFO advisory and the COA design belong in the same engagement. Common Pitfalls The recurring SaaS chart-of-accounts mistakes are predictable, and most trace back to using a generic template instead of a SaaS-built one. Each one distorts a number that someone in diligence will eventually reclassify. Hosting in operating expense instead of COGS. AWS and GCP production spend is cost of revenue. Put it in OpEx and your reported gross margin inflates, then evaporates the moment a diligence team moves it, per The SaaS CFO . The consequence is a margin that fails due diligence. No expansion-versus-new revenue separation. One blended revenue account makes NRR, GRR, and NDR impossible to compute from the ledger, per ChartMogul . The consequence is broken retention analysis the night before a board meeting. Sales commissions misclassified as COGS. Commissions are a selling expense, not a cost of delivering the product, per DualEntry . The consequence is inflated COGS and deflated gross margin. No deferred revenue account. Collecting annual prepayments without a deferred revenue liability recognizes revenue prematurely. The consequence is a clear ASC 606 violation and an audit red flag. No current-versus-long-term split on deferred revenue. A single deferred revenue account obscures the within-12-months versus beyond-12-months presentation auditors expect. The consequence is an audit finding on balance-sheet classification. S&M lumped with G&A. The consequence is dead magic-number, CAC-payback, and Rule of 40 analysis, because all three are computed off isolated S&M. Over-granular accounts nobody maintains. A 200-account chart that gets miscoded is worse than a 60-account chart coded correctly, per Kruze Consulting . The consequence is a chart that drifts and reclassification work after a tax period closes. Most generalist firms miss these until an auditor flags them. Indinero’s books are audit-ready by default, because GAAP discipline is baked into how the team operates, not added later. The CPA team catches the misclassification during monthly close review, before it reaches a data room. The Audit-Ready Standard An audit-ready SaaS chart of accounts is one where the financial statements roll up directly from the ledger with no off-system reclassification, every ASC 606 contract liability and contract asset is presented per ASC 606-10-45-1 through -3, and the revenue and cost segmentation serves both GAAP and the SaaS metrics in one structure. In practice, three things hold true. First, classification matches the standards. Deferred revenue is a contract liability presented net per ASC 606-10-45-1, split current and long-term. Contract assets are presented separately from receivables per ASC 606-10-45-3. Capitalized commissions sit as deferred costs under ASC 340-40, and capitalized development as an intangible under ASC 350-40, each with amortization flowing to the right line. Second, the chart was built before the transactions, not reverse-engineered after. The expensive version of this work is recategorizing historical transactions, which gets genuinely painful once a tax period has closed. Series A audit prep should be months of clean books, not weeks of scramble to reclassify two years of miscoded hosting spend. Our audit preparation walkthrough covers what that readiness looks like in practice. Third, the same chart serves GAAP and the board deck. Revenue segmented for ASC 606 is the same segmentation that produces NRR and GRR. Cost isolated for gross margin is the same data the Rule of 40 needs. When the COA is built once, correctly, the audit, the tax return, the R&D credit base, and the investor metrics all draw from one source of truth. Build it right the first time. How indinero Approaches the SaaS COA Indinero’s CPA team builds the SaaS chart of accounts inside the tooling you already run, then maintains it as part of monthly close. The structure above is not a one-time setup deliverable. It is a living chart that has to stay correct every month as new revenue streams, products, and entities appear, which is where most internally maintained charts drift. The GAAP discipline is handled upfront, so your month-end close runs in roughly 5 days instead of 45, and your audit prep is months of clean books instead of weeks of scramble. The SaaS COA is the foundation of that. Revenue segmented for ASC 606, hosting seated in COGS, S&M separated from G&A, and deferred revenue split current and long-term, all built and maintained so the statements roll up clean. There is no platform to migrate to. Indinero builds and maintains the chart of accounts inside QuickBooks Online or NetSuite, integrating with the stack you already use, with no proprietary lock-in. The accounting services scope covers the full monthly GAAP-compliant close, financial statement preparation across the P&L, balance sheet, cash flow, and statement of equity, cash-to-accrual conversion, multi-entity consolidation, ASC 606 revenue recognition, and audit prep and support. The structural difference from a tool-only or bench-style provider is that the chart is built by CPAs and bundled with tax and fractional CFO under one monthly engagement. The same team that designs the revenue segmentation knows it has to feed the R&D credit base and the Section 174A treatment, because the same engagement files the return. Indinero has run continuously since 2009 under stable ownership, holds a 5-star Clutch rating, serves 500+ regular customers, is SOC 2 compliant (2026), and offers month-to-month engagements with pricing that starts at $750/mo. For a growth-stage SaaS company heading into a Series A audit, the question is rarely whether you have a chart of accounts. It is whether the one you have was built to survive scrutiny. If you want a SaaS COA built right from day one, reach out for a free consultation . We’d love to learn about your business and find where we can help. Frequently asked questions Founders and finance leaders ask the same questions when they sit down to structure or restructure a SaaS chart of accounts. The answers below are grounded in the structure above and the work Indinero’s CPA team does building and maintaining audit-ready charts of accounts for growth-stage SaaS companies inside QuickBooks Online and NetSuite. Why do SaaS companies need a different chart of accounts than a traditional services business? A SaaS chart of accounts carries deferred revenue, accrued revenue, deferred cost of revenue, and hosting COGS that a traditional services COA never needs. Software revenue splits recurring subscription from one-time services and usage, and cost of revenue is dominated by cloud hosting rather than raw materials or inventory. An analyst should be able to read your business model straight off the chart, which a generic QuickBooks default template with one undifferentiated Sales account cannot deliver. How granular should revenue accounts be in a SaaS COA? SaaS revenue should be segmented by recognition pattern, typically subscription, expansion, usage, implementation, professional services, and a contra-revenue line. Each stream maps to a different ASC 606 treatment, so blending them into one Revenue account is both an audit failure and an analytics failure. Expansion needs its own account specifically so net revenue retention and gross revenue retention can be computed directly from the ledger. That metric only exists if the COA was built to produce it. Should hosting costs go in COGS or operating expenses? Hosting and cloud infrastructure for production environments belong in COGS, because they are a direct cost of delivering the running product to existing customers. The rule is mechanical. If a cost is incurred to deliver the product, it is cost of revenue, and if it is incurred to build, sell, or run the company, it is operating expense. Drop hosting into OpEx and your gross margin reads artificially high, then evaporates the moment a diligence team reclassifies it. How do I structure S&M, R&D, and G&A for SaaS-style operating expense reporting? Split operating expense into R&D, S&M, and G&A, and place Customer Success in COGS or G&A based on its role. R&D carries engineering wages, dev tooling, and contractor engineering. S&M holds sales wages, commissions, advertising, and events. G&A covers exec, finance, HR, legal, rent, and insurance. Keeping S&M isolated from G&A is what makes the magic number, CAC payback, and Rule of 40 computable from the ledger. When should I add departmental tags or classes to the COA? Add departmental tags or classes once you need expense reporting by function or entity that account numbering alone cannot capture. That inflection usually arrives around Series B, as the chart reaches 80 to 100 accounts. Seed-stage companies run lean at 30 to 40 accounts, and Series A expands to 50 to 70 with revenue and COGS detail. The structure stays constant while granularity grows. Add tags before the sprawl, not after, so departmental P&L rolls up without manual reclassification. How do I avoid breaking historical comparability when I restructure the COA? Leave numbering gaps between accounts so related lines insert later without renumbering history, and use parent and child subaccounts instead of a flat sprawl. If your COGS accounts run 5000 to 5050, start the next band at 5100, not 5051. Restructuring after a tax period has closed means recategorizing historical transactions, which is the expensive version of this work. Indinero’s CPA team builds the chart before the transactions and maintains it during monthly close, so prior periods stay comparable. Does QuickBooks Online or NetSuite affect how I structure the COA? QuickBooks Online and NetSuite share the same four-digit numbering logic, so the classification structure of a SaaS COA stays identical across both tools. NetSuite assigns all 1-series accounts to assets and 2-series to liabilities, and QuickBooks Online uses the same four-digit default once account numbers are enabled. Subaccount syntax differs, with QuickBooks writing Hosting:AWS and NetSuite pointing a child at its parent. Indinero builds and maintains the chart inside whichever you already run, with no proprietary platform to migrate to.

title: Canterbury Park Hall of Fame Adds Three Members; Regulator Dr. Camille McArdle, owner Pete Mattson, quarter horse Dickey Bob join MN racing’s elite
summary: The Canterbury Park Hall of Fame will induct three new members in a ceremony to be held Friday, July 24 as part of Hall of Fame Weekend at the Shakopee, Minn. racetrack. The Class of 2026 includes thoroughbred owner and breeder Pete Mattson, all-time leading money earning Minnesota-bred quarter horse Dickey Bob and former chief […]
body_text: The Canterbury Park Hall of Fame will induct three new members in a ceremony to be held Friday, July 24 as part of Hall of Fame Weekend at the Shakopee, Minn. racetrack. The Class of 2026 includes thoroughbred owner and breeder Pete Mattson, all-time leading money earning Minnesota-bred quarter horse Dickey Bob and former chief veterinarian and Minnesota Racing Commission chair Dr. Camille McArdle. The three join a group of more than 50 individuals and horses that comprise the best of Minnesota horse racing. The green “MHC” silks of Mattson’s stable combine two important facets of his life – his business and horse racing. Carried to victory by Minnesota-bred stakes winners Fireman Oscar, Doctor Pete Mattson and Jareth Loveberry Oscar, Astronaut Oscar, Retired Kathy, Molly’s Angel, Thealligatorhunter, Summer Winner and more, the biggest days at Canterbury Park were some of the best for Mattson. From his first win with a partnership in 1991 with Wild Moose Chase, to solo-owned winner Dazzle Baby in 2002, to an exciting debut win by home-bred Mighty Samurai in 2026, Mattson’s support and success at Canterbury spans more than three decades. Dickey Bob Dickey Bob’s first win as a 2-year-old and his final win at the age of 10 both came at Canterbury Park. There were 30 additional wins in between at multiple tracks for the son of Apollitical Jess at distances ranging from 110 yards to 400 yards. Out of the mare Paint or More, Dickey Bob is the richest of seven full siblings who combined earned nearly $1.5 million. Owned and bred by Bruce and Judy Lunderborg’s Lunderborg LLC, Dickey Bob retired last year and is living on trainer Jason Olmstead’s farm. His $529,119 in earnings over 70 races is the most ever by a Minnesota-bred quarter horse. In 1985, Dr. McArdle was named the MRC’s first chief veterinarian for the fledgling industry. She built the veterinary department around these core principles: protecting horses’ health and the integrity of the sport. In 1993, Dr. McArdle was appointed to the Racing Commission during a time of transition. She provided steady leadership after the closure of Canterbury Downs at the end of 1992, then helped guide the sport into a new era with the opening of Canterbury Park in 1994. Serving under five governors over 41 years, she was named commission chair in 2021. Dr. McArdle resigned from the commission in 2025 after state government officials rejected her efforts to help Canterbury Park and Running Aces add new sources of purse revenue. Dr. McArdle The Canterbury Park Hall of Fame was founded in 1995 to recognize people and horses that have made important and lasting contributions to the racing industry within the state. The selection committee consists of representatives of local horsemen organizations, media, and Canterbury Park.

title: HR Pulse: How to Create a Resume That Passes AI Screening and Still Sounds Like You
summary: In this article, we break down common myths about AI screening, explain why strong resumes still get filtered out, and outline practical ways to create a CV that works for both technology and people.
body_text: Employers are increasingly looking for resumes that balance the right format, targeted keywords, measurable achievements, and a mix of hard and soft skills that match the role. Creating an AI-friendly resume does not mean letting AI do all the work for you. AI tools can help job seekers move faster but overusing them can lead to resumes that sound generic, rely too heavily on keywords, or fail to reflect the candidate’s real strengths and voice. The goal is not to ‘beat the system.’ It is to build a resume that is decipherable by technology and convincing to people. In this article, we break down common myths about AI screening, explain why strong resumes still get filtered out, and outline practical ways to create a CV that works for both technology and people. To understand how AI really affects hiring decisions, it helps to clear up a few common misconceptions. Myth 1: AI automatically rejects resumes Reality: Resumes are filtered out when they are unclear, misaligned, or when application questions are answered incorrectly, not because an algorithm “rejected” the candidate . Section 1: Making Your Resume Stand Out in the Age of AI: Formatting and Tailoring Tips As AI-powered tools and Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) play a larger role in the hiring process, job seekers need to be more intentional about how they present their experience. The right formatting and a tailored approach ensure both the technology and the humans behind the process can clearly understand your qualifications. Here’s how candidates can make their resumes stand out Use Clean, ATS-Friendly Formatting AI systems work best with simple, consistent resume structures. Clear section headers such as work experience, skills, and education help parsing tools identify key information quickly. Candidates should avoid text boxes, columns, graphics, and decorative elements that many systems struggle to interpret. Myth 2: Creative designs impress AI Reality: Most screening tools prioritize structure over style. Visual elements such as tables, graphics, or text boxes can confuse and interrupt how information is parsed. A simple, conventional layout helps ensure your experience is captured accurately before a recruiter ever sees it. Standard, readable fonts, like Arial, Calibri, or Times New Roman, are recommended, and saving your resume as a Word (.docx) file is often recommended for maximum compatibility, however many systems also accept well-structured PDFs. Important details, including contact information and job titles, should always appear in the main body of the resume, not in headers or footers. Simple bullet points are easier for AI to read than decorative symbols, and traditional chronological or hybrid formats remain the most effective. Creative or overly visual layouts may appeal to the eye but can be misread, or skipped entirely, by screening tools. Tailor Your Resume to Each Job Description In the age of AI screening, tailoring a resume isn’t optional, it is one of the most effective ways to move forward in the hiring process. Modern ATS and AI tools compare resumes directly with the job description, scanning for key skills, terminology, and experience. When a resume naturally incorporates the same language used in the posting, it’s more likely to pass initial filters. Tailoring also helps candidates highlight their most relevant strengths. By adjusting bullet points and emphasizing accomplishments that align with the role, applicants make it easier for both automated systems and hiring managers to see why they are a strong fit. This approach keeps the resume focused, reduces irrelevant information, and signals genuine interest in the specific position. Section 2: Why Some Resumes Don’t Make It Past AI Screening Even with strong experience and good intentions, many resumes fail not because of substance, but because of how they are interpreted by screening systems. If you have been applying to jobs and hearing little to nothing back, the issue may not be your qualifications, it may be how your resume is being processed. Today's ATSs and AI-powered tools don’t read resumes like humans do; instead, they scan for specific keywords, structure, and data points. If your resume isn’t aligned with how these systems work, it can be filtered out within seconds. One of the most common reasons resumes are rejected is the lack of relevant keywords. AI tools are designed to match resumes to job descriptions, so if your resume doesn’t include the same terminology such as specific skills, tools, or job titles it may not rank high enough to move forward. Even if your experience is strong, using different phrasing from what appears in the job description can cause the system to overlook your qualifications. Myth 3: More keywords always improve your chances Reality: Overuse of keywords can actually hurt your resume. AI screening tools look for context and relevance, not repetition. Keywords work best when they are naturally embedded in clear results, focused experience that aligns with the role. Another issue may be unclear or non-traditional structure. As mentioned previously, AI systems are programmed to recognize standard resume sections such as work experience, education, and skills. When these headings are replaced with more creative titles, the system may struggle to categorize your information correctly. This can impact how your resume is ranked, even if the content itself is strong. Ultimately, getting rejected doesn’t always mean you do not have the qualifications. More often, it means your resume isn’t optimized for how AI evaluates candidates. By understanding how these systems work, you can better position your experience to be seen, understood, and moved forward in the hiring process. Section 3: Level up! What Makes a CV AI-Friendly Understanding why resumes fall short is the first step. The next is applying that insight to deliberately strengthen how your experience is presented. Leveling up your resume today is less about adding more, and more about presenting your experience more clearly, strategically, and with impact. One of the most effective ways to improve your resume is by using AI tools to better understand how your experience is being presented. It is important to find the right balance between being AI friendly and appealing to what a recruiter is actually looking for. Your resume should be clear, relevant, and still feel authentic to you. Myth 4: Using AI guarantees a stronger resume Reality: AI improves efficiency, not judgment. AI can help draft, refine, and tailor content, but resumes perform best when candidates review, personalize, and validate every line to ensure accuracy, credibility, and authentic voice. Focus on results, not just responsibilities Metrics are highly valued by both AI systems and recruiters, so highlighting outcomes such as percentages, growth, or efficiency improvements can significantly strengthen your resume. Even small contributions can help show value when framed the right way. Here’s what that difference can look like in practice: Before: Responsible for onboarding new employees. After: Improved employee onboarding completion rates by 30% by redesigning training materials and delivery format. Before: Assisted with event planning. After: Supported planning and execution of five campus events attended by 250+ participants, coordinating logistics and communications. Use AI as a support, not a shortcut. Use specific language to explain what you have done and how you have done it, including the systems or technologies involved. While AI can help polish and structure your resume, it should never create experience, exaggerate results, or make decisions on your behalf. Be intentional, not automated. It’s understandable to want to apply quickly to many roles, but mass application tools can work against you. Many employers can spot automated submissions and deprioritize them. Focusing instead on roles that genuinely interest you, and applying thoughtfully, often leads to better response rates and more meaningful conversations. At the end of the day, an AI friendly resume is not about gaming the system. It is about presenting your experience in a way that is easy for technology to read and compelling for a recruiter to move forward. Self-Assessment: Is Your Resume AI Aware and Human ready? Here is a checklist you can run through before applying for your next position. It is designed to help you evaluate clarity, credibility, and alignment, and to avoid using only keyword coverage. 1. Structure & Readability I have used standard section headings (e.g., Work experience, skills, education). My resume follows a simple, single column layout. Important details, contact info, job titles, dates, appear in the main body and not in the headers or footers. 2. Relevance & Language My resume reflects the language used in the job description without copying it directly. I describe my experience using specific tools, systems, or processes where applicable. My skills section reinforces what is shown in my experience without duplication. 3. Impact & Credibility Bullet points show outcomes, results, or improvements. Any metrics I include are accurate and justifiable. My descriptions explain what I actually contributed, not only a team or department mandate. 4. AI Use & Authenticity If I used AI tools, I reviewed and edited the language to match my voice. No bullet point feels vague, inflated, or disconnected from my real experience. I can confidently explain every line in an interview. 5. Final Check If AI screening were not involved, this resume would still clearly tell my story. A recruiter could understand my role, value, and strengths in under one minute. Note: This self-assessment is designed as a reflective tool, to help job seekers balance AI screening requirements with clear ‑human-centered‑ storytelling. “ Just as resumes today are read by both technology and people, the most effective candidates are those who design for both without losing their voice.” Human Experience, Strategically Presented AI is changing the job search, but the fundamentals of a strong resume still matter. Clear formatting, relevant keywords, measurable accomplishments, strong contact information, and a thoughtful mix of hard and soft skills can all improve the chances that your resume is successfully parsed and seriously considered. A resume summary and tailored language can also help show alignment with the role without sacrificing clarity. As AI becomes a standard part of hiring, the resumes that stand out will be those that pair thoughtful optimization with genuine voice. Job seekers who succeed will be intentional in how they tailor their materials, using AI as a support, while staying firmly in control of their story, tone, and credibility. title: 3M and Microsoft announce strategic partnership to advance AI data center infrastructure and enterprise transformation
summary: The post 3M and Microsoft announce strategic partnership to advance AI data center infrastructure and enterprise transformation appeared first on Source .
body_text: Microsoft becomes first announced hyperscale cloud provider to deploy 3M Expanded Beam Optical (EBO) technology 3M to use Microsoft AI and digital capabilities to advance enterprise transformation across key functions ST. PAUL, Minn. and REDMOND, Wash. — July 15, 2026 — 3M (NYSE: MMM) and Microsoft (Nasdaq: MSFT) today announced a strategic partnership focused on AI data center infrastructure and enterprise transformation. Microsoft’s Azure cloud and AI infrastructure will become the first announced hyperscale cloud provider to deploy 3M’s Expanded Beam Optical (EBO) technology. 3M will also use Microsoft’s AI and digital platforms as part of its enterprise transformation across key business functions. Together, the companies will combine Microsoft’s digital and hyperscale infrastructure with 3M’s materials science and precision manufacturing to accelerate AI adoption and strengthen the physical networks required for the growth of cloud and AI workloads. Innovating datacenter infrastructure for the AI era As Microsoft continues to advance high-performance, efficient and sustainable infrastructure for enterprise and generative AI workloads, it will deploy 3M’s proprietary EBO technology in Azure data centers. By using an expanded beam optical interface instead of the direct contact required in traditional connectors, EBO technology is designed to make fiber connections faster to install, more tolerant of contamination and easier to maintain. The technology will help Microsoft reduce the need for frequent cleaning and inspection while supporting reliable optical performance in dense, high-volume deployment environments. Microsoft’s early use of EBO technology has shown the potential to reduce network deployment timelines in certain environments. The technology has also demonstrated strong signal performance in live data center conditions, where dust exposure and routine handling are typical during installation and maintenance. 3M is scaling production of its EBO technology to meet accelerating demand from hyperscalers and data center operators building the infrastructure required for AI. Building on decades of materials science and precision-manufacturing expertise, 3M has advanced single-mode expanded beam optical technology for high-volume data center applications, supporting disciplined commercialization and broader adoption across the data center ecosystem. 3M helped establish the EBO Multi-Source Agreement (MSA) to support standardization and broader industry adoption of EBO technology. “At Microsoft, we’re redefining the foundation of cloud and AI infrastructure — combining our own innovations with advances from partners like 3M to build datacenters that are faster to deploy, more resilient and ready for the scale of AI,” said Cliff Henson, corporate vice president, cloud supply chain and engineering at Microsoft. “3M’s EBO solution will help unlock new levels of performance, reliability and efficiency to ensure customers can run their cloud and AI workloads on a trusted, sustainable and advanced environment.” Enterprise AI transformation 3M will deploy Microsoft’s AI and digital capabilities in key areas of its enterprise transformation road map, including customer service, finance, sales and marketing. These efforts will help simplify processes, improve decision-making, strengthen customer experiences and enable greater employee productivity. A specific example involves the newly launched Microsoft Frontier Company deploying engineers to help 3M’s Global Business Services team automate the way it manages customer orders. Both companies are collaborating on an AI agent–driven workflow to assist with credit checks, delinquency assessments and system updates, with human-in-the-loop controls and a custom monitoring dashboard for real-time visibility and approvals. This solution is expected to significantly reduce manual effort, improve process speed and consistency, and accelerate cash flow, freeing 3M staff for higher-value work and enabling scalable, auditable operations. “At 3M, we view AI as a powerful tool that can accelerate growth, improve customer experiences and help our teams work more effectively,” said Jon Van Wyck, executive vice president and chief strategy officer, 3M. “Our collaboration with Microsoft supports that vision through targeted optimization opportunities for our enterprise while advancing the infrastructure needed to power the future of AI. We are excited to deepen our partnership and develop practical solutions that can create mutual value.” Building the future through science and technology Microsoft and 3M intend to build on this partnership through continued technical collaboration, bench-to-bench engagement between engineering and commercial teams, and joint innovation opportunities across Microsoft’s data center and device ecosystem, with a focus on areas where 3M’s materials science, optical connectivity and manufacturing capabilities can help address evolving requirements for reliability, deployment speed, density and long-term scalability. About 3M 3M (NYSE: MMM) is focused on transforming industries around the world by applying science and creating innovative, customer-focused solutions. Our multi-disciplinary team is working to solve tough customer problems by leveraging diverse technology platforms, differentiated capabilities, global footprint and operational excellence. Discover how 3M is shaping the future at 3M.com/news . About Microsoft Microsoft (Nasdaq “MSFT” @microsoft) creates platforms and tools powered by AI to deliver innovative solutions that meet the evolving needs of our customers. The technology company is committed to making AI available broadly and doing so responsibly, with a mission to empower every person and every organization on the planet to achieve more.
